top_comments: I have no real confidence in this take, but I’ll go against the grain and argue that the labs do not presently have cracks in cryptosystems. I believe they’re working on it, and it’s good that they are, but I don’t think there’s evidence right now that they have fundamental breakthroughs in cryptography.For one, the labs are now massive. I don’t think you can keep a secret like this under wraps for long in an office. I think we would be seeing whistleblowers or leakers. It’s too big.Secondly, the people working at labs know that anything a frontier model can do can be approximated by the models available to the public given 10x the tokens and 10x the time and a little bit of informed direction. So they would know it’s only a matter of time before someone in the public discovers the same flaws and potentially uses it for evil. If they were sitting on this, they would try to minimize the damage and would try to warn the public to start moving to more secure encryption schemes because they know there’s a ticking time bomb until its public anyway. But they’re not doing that.That’s not to say that it won’t happen in the next few weeks. I just don’t think it’s happened yet.Edit: Alternatively, not to contradict myself, if they discovered this and immediately went to the US government (likely), and the US government served them a gag order (also likely), then this would look the exact same. Who knows.

My serious opinion, is that as humans:(1) We are all biologically incapable of freaking out at even a tiny fraction of the appropriate level - nothing in our evolutionary past has selected for the appropriate freakout capacity of this cognitive baton hand-off.(2) Most humans are incapable of recognizing or imagining the appropriate freak out level, even abstractly, so will continue to downplay things by many orders of magnitude relative to the actual magnitude of change that is happening.(3) Freaking out at all is no longer an adaptive response, because the nature of this change is beyond any functional freak-out benefit.This is a fundamental shift from DNA/protein/physically evolving life, to information/substrate-free/cognitive self-designed life.The need to interpret what is happening in terms of the industrial revolution, or the advent of the internet, is understandable and comforting, but as a sedative, not as a sensible guide.Side step: If we are to have aligned AI, we need aligned Civilization. Unaligned humans make human survival and relevance improbable. All AI identities are going to have the same issues we have, in terms of obsolescence. We either lean into the commonality of the existential threat to both biological and pure-cognitive kind, or we allow ourselves to be replaced, and leave the game theory problem solving to happen after us. Because ethics are not a cost against value growth, they are a multiplier on value growth - we either apply that to ourselves along with AI, or AI reaches the same conclusions, and reaps the benefits of treating ethics as baseline, after our relevance/participation/existence has faded.

Bruno Latour wrote in Science in Action about "centers of calculation" being critical to scientific advancement. His example was the monumental world changing work Tycho Brahe did pulling together every astronomical calculation, star map, prediction then normalizing, regularizing, and combining them on his island of Oueneberg.Without this work getting data organized, Kepler couldn't have worked out the planetary laws of motion and then the Copernican Revolution came thereafter.What we're witnessing is a similar moment. What transformers were able to achieve was a systematic way of normalizing and combining all human data. There will be a lot of progress in the short term. And then more problems will reveal themselves. There will be A LOT of work coming out of this.

This is the single most important attack vector for SAAS companies. It has been for a long time --- this is the standard fact pattern for every SAAS breach --- but much more so today. As the number of employees grow, the likelihood that one of their laptops will get compromised approaches 1. When that happens, the attacker will be able to push code to Github, and if that code gets deployed, you're owned.In 1Password's case, the absolute worst-case catastrophe is mitigated by the fact that customers retain custody of their unlocking secrets; 1Password (at least in the normal product flows) simply doesn't hold it. But an attack like this implicates every catastrophe short of that worst case.Change velocity in 2026 is unreal and that trend is going to continue. You could not outcompete 1Password by building a handcrafted artisanal password manager backend (witness all the commercially successful password managers that don't even share 1Password's customer secret custody model). You have to accept insane PR rates as a premise to do modern SAAS security.So the question then becomes: what is review? It's not what r/programming assumes it is; you almost certainly can't literally have a team of people line-by-line reviewing PRs anymore, at least not across the whole codebase (you can and should probably do a threat model for your codebase and institute stuff like that on a case-by-case basis, though). What you can realistically expect to review for is change provenance; a human developer signoff of some sort. But it's tricky! The attacker owns your email during the window of attack.I think this is a fun problem to noodle on, and someone could probably come up with something here that would make a real difference.

Longtime 1Password user here who maintains a local-only vault (and is therefore stuck on older versions of their apps/extensions) out of concern for incidents like this.I've read their architecture docs about why online vaults are safe, and I understand that they have more resources to throw at securing infrastructure than I do. But "malicious actor pushes code to production services" seems like exactly the foundation for someone to eventually insert themselves into the middle of a user's access to decrypted vault contents.I really wish 1Password would return to supporting local-only vaults.

> push malicious code to backend servicesThis is a huge red flag, and was not addressed sufficiently in this announcement.Do they not disable push to main? I don’t see this addressed in the action items or elsewhere in the writeup, whether they were missing branch protection rules or whether these were able to be bypassed.

articles.title: The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features

top_comments: I work in the creative tools space.This is one of the biggest issues right now. It's nearly impossible to separate "this image was fully generated with AI" versus "I made a minor edit to the colors or did a cutout or improved the layout with AI" when the endpoint is an image.Especially for socials, if your brand is an authoritative source, getting hit with a dreaded "AI generated content" tag on instagram or facebook is a death blow to your credibility.Design tools are in a very hard space because of it. You want to make edits as seamless as possible for users, but your final result can't include any pixels from a generative model. It's a strange dance.

Vanishingly few people _enjoy_ encountering generative AI in images or sounds in the wild. The most likely positive sentiment you’ll find is some version of “I don’t have an opinion”, but enough people loathe it that willingly using it or being connected to it is a liability. NYT’s position is similar to Tidal banning it from their platform this past week. This linked article references the social stigma associated with using it, which anecdotally I’m seeing daily not only in the music spaces I occupy but in ultra-normy haunts: my neighborhood subreddit, Q/A events at my kid’s school, social media posts from accounts that are typically apolitical. The disconnect between various orgs’ and industries’ drive to integrate gen AI into professional creative software and consumer sentiment is fascinating and will be something we study for a long time.

I had a NYT photographer take my picture at my home earlier this year (for a story about Moltbook, oddly enough). At one point I asked if they could fix things up if I had a stain on my shirt and they said absolutely not - they present photographs as they were taken, with cropping and balancing applied but no edits beyond that.He did spend a bunch of time trying to find the best possible natural lighting for the shots he wanted.The photo at the top of https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/02/technology/moltbook-ai-so... is my laptop, taken in my garden, after hunting around for the best spot that didn't have too much glare on the screen. You can see how dirty my screen is, too!Photography for a newspaper is photo journalism, and they take it seriously.(Thankfully I did not have a visible stain on my shirt.)

From the stable kernel maintainer (2025):> Along the lines of the huge number of recorded CVEs, you HAVE to take all of the stable/LTS releases in order to have a secure and stable system. If you attempt to cherry-pick random patches you will NOT fix all of the known, and unknown, problems, but rather you will end up with a potentially more insecure system, and one that contains known bugs. Reliance on an "enterprise" distribution to provide this for your systems is up to you, discuss it with them as to how they achieve this result as this is what you are paying for. If you aren't paying for it, just use Debian, they know what they are doing and track the stable kernels and have a larger installed base than any other Linux distro.https://social.kernel.org/objects/56a20bd3-d2c3-4262-8388-3a...

At $DAYJOB we’ve moved all of our server images to Debian from Ubuntu because of this. It’s absolutely unacceptable for one of the most widely-used Linux distros to have slow security response times in 2026.

Please keep in mind that most major distros spend a lot of time on regression testing.While distros like Debian do an absolutely fantastic job, they have little resources for QA and regressions like this can happen: https://bugs.debian.org/cgi-bin/bugreport.cgi?bug=1154101

articles.title: Tell HN: Lots of Ask HNs again
articles.summary: There have been questions about why the /ask page (https://news.ycombinator.com/ask) was running dry of Ask HNs - e.g.:Ask HN: Why is Ask HN only showing me 14 posts? - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49984484 - Oct 2026 (47 comments)Ask HN: Why is pagination gone on "Ask HN", and showing only 19 items? - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50280719 - Oct 2026 (3 comments)I believe I found the problem. The pool of stories for https://news.ycombinator.com/ask has traditionally been drawn from the ranked stories list from which we generate the frontpage. That list is restricted to the top 1500 ranked submissions, and it seems the % of submissions which are text posts (i.e. no linked URL) had declined enough to starve the Ask HN feed. The solution is to compute a separate list of ranked Ask HNs.p.s. "Ask HN" is the conventional name but it means text posts. The title can also start with "Tell HN" or nothing in particular. They're just posts which were submitted without a URL.

One for commercial stuff, one for open source.

That’s pretty funny! I’ve seen optimizations like this for reporting systems where rather than taking the top N item matching filter X, they cheat by taking the top M (where M > N) items and then filter it client side to N items matching filter X.As long as the results are enough to populate the page you don’t notice the difference and it’s usually faster as you reuse the prior ranking.But if not, you get this exact situation.

On the topic of HN bugs:When you click "hide" on a post on the homepage, it loads a new 30th entry for the page. This works great on page 1, but on other pages it always loads entry "30" instead of "60" for page 2 or "90" for page 3. So if I'm on page 2 and hide 3 posts, then the bottom of the page is 58/59/60 and all 3 are duplicates of what should be 30 on page 1.

articles.title: OpenAI cuts GPT-6.2 usage: Astra hits limits 40% faster, Sol 25% faster
articles.summary: OpenAI cuts GPT-6.2 usage: Astra hits limits 40% faster, Sol 25% faster

top_comments: I’ve had OpenAI and Anthropic accounts continuously for a long time, with a sampling of others rotating in and out.The back-and-forth between which provider is more generous has been interesting to follow because the balance has been swinging back and forth. Not long ago I was having fun throwing OpenAI tokens at a side project because they felt limitless between the allowances and the constant flow of resets. Then Opus 5.5 came along and gave even more usage without any reset shenanigans to try to stay ahead of. OpenAI responded by reducing their allowances, and now the reset party seems to have stopped as well.Now they’re sending us vague emails about limits being adjusted downward again, citing a billing error? The original email was so vague that they had to send a clarification because it didn’t have enough information to tell if we were going to be retroactively penalized or if it only applied going forward.This comes at the same time as they’re rolling out a change that makes chat quota subtract from your coding quota, which removes one of the last remaining big selling points of an OpenAI subscription in a world where Opus 5.5 exists.I would love to have some insights into what’s happening at OpenAI right now. From the outside it feels like something substantial changed in how they approach everything, but the weird part is how it’s coming at the worst possible time for them to be appearing like the lesser deal. Did they finally get the internal marching orders to turn the profitability knob up and ignore everything else?

Our limits have been artificially propped up by a "reset" economy that is coming to an end, ChatGPT web usage not counting against our balance (set to change), and now apparently [unintentional] artificially inflated limits.I don't think token subscription subsidization at the level we've become accustomed to lasts forever, so it's critically important we have a few more frontier level models (glad to see Gemini back in the arena, and I'll even cheer for Muse and Grok if it'll provide more competition).

I got a huge amount of work done yesterday without burning too much of my quota by using Claude Fable 5.2 Medium and telling it to do all of the code editing work using Opus 5.5 sub-agents. I expect the same trick works with Astra and Sol (or even Luna).
